subtype: Approach: talking to current employees at both firms [Action]
passage: Note by Jagdish, mentor. On Monday Rashmi showed me two messages she had sent through a professional network, one to an engineer at each firm that had offered her a job. Each asked the same three things: how heavy the workload gets, how much people learn, and how appraisals work. By Wednesday both had replied. One wrote that sprints end late on Thursdays, learning is mostly on your own, and appraisal comes once a year. The other described weekly code reviews, a small course budget, and appraisal every six months. Rashmi copied both answers into a table. "None of this was in the offer letters," she said. I suggested nothing. She will ask each HR team about appraisal timing before Friday.

qa.q: Which three things did Rashmi ask each employee?
qa.a: She asked how heavy the workload gets, how much people learn, and how appraisals work.

qa.q: What is Rashmi feeling as she copies the replies into a table?
qa.a: She seems relieved and curious: she says none of this was in the offer letters, and she is glad to have real details.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rashmi try to check what she heard, and why?
qa.a: She could ask each HR team the same questions in writing, because two individual views may be a little biased and an official reply is easier to compare.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see Rashmi's approach?
qa.a: Jagdish watches a graduate collecting facts before choosing, and holds back suggestions so that the decision stays with Rashmi.

grounding: Shows a graduate contacting current employees at two firms and learning details about work, learning and appraisal that the offer letters omit.
